query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A phase‐selective recrystallization annealing treatment that targets the ductile phase within the dual-phase lamellar microstructure will reduce dislocation pile‐ups at the internal phase boundaries. By locally recrystallizing and refining the ductile (soft) phase while preserving the hard phase network, the treatment is expected to lower stress concentrations that lead to microcrack initiation, thereby enhancing room-temperature tensile ductility while retaining or slightly increasing the alloy’s strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy possessing a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, where a ductile (soft) phase is interwoven with a reinforcing hard phase network. In this state, severe dislocation accumulation at the phase boundaries causes local stress concentrations and brittleness.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled, short-duration annealing treatment designed to induce phase-selective recrystallization of the ductile phase without coarsening the hard phase.
generation.conditions: Quasi-static room-temperature tensile testing; the annealing process is executed under an inert atmosphere with precisely tailored temperature and time to selectively recrystallize the soft phase.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined ductile phase with smoother and more coherent internal boundaries embedded in a largely unaltered hard phase network.
generation.mechanism: Selective recrystallization alleviates dislocation pile-ups by replacing the heavily deformed ductile phase with a recrystallized, finer grained structure that mitigates local stress concentrations. This modification delays the initiation of microcracks at internal interfaces while the preserved hard phase sustains or slightly enhances overall strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: An improvement in uniform tensile ductility (as indicated by increased elongation to failure) accompanied by retention or a modest increase in yield and ultimate tensile strengths relative to the untreated alloy.
generation.baseline: The untreated eutectic HEA exhibits limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittle failure due to severe dislocation accumulation at internal phase boundaries.
generation.boundary: The improvement is highly sensitive to the annealing parameters; overly aggressive treatment may induce excessive grain growth or loss of the hard phase connectivity, which could compromise the strength.
generation.uncertainty: While enhanced ductility is anticipated, the exact magnitude of improvement and the optimal balance between ductility and strength depend on the precise control of the annealing conditions and require further experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of the eutectic HEA samples: one set undergoing the optimized phase-selective annealing treatment and a control set remaining untreated. Characterize the microstructure using TEM and EBSD to confirm selective recrystallization of the ductile phase and minimal hard phase alteration, then subject both sets to quasi-static room-temperature tensile tests.
measurements: TEM/EBSD imaging for grain size and phase mapping of the ductile region
Quantification of dislocation densities and pile-up patterns at the phase boundaries
Tensile stress–strain curves measuring yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation to failure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit a significantly refined ductile phase with reduced dislocation pile-ups at the internal boundaries, or if there is no measurable improvement in tensile ductility (and/or if strength is compromised) compared to the untreated samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs), which are composed of five to 13 main elements, with each element’s content 5–35 at %, have been studied for more than 10 years, ever since they were first defined in 2004 []. Usually, HEAs are composed of either single or multiple body-centered cubic (BCC) or face-centered cubic (FCC) phases, and most of the investigations reported have focused on single phase alloys []. Recently, a dual phase AlCoCrFeNi HEA was prepared by arc melting and homogenization heat treatment []. Results showed that the precipitation of the FCC phase at the BCC grain boundaries reflected the effect of the FCC phase on crack deflection and branching during propagation under tensile loading. It was found that the presence of a ductile FCC high-entropy phase can impart good room temperature ductility to the brittle BCC phase. The excellent comprehensive performance, which includes its high strength, high hardness, good wear resistance, and good thermal stability, make HEAs promising industrial structural materials that can replace the traditional ones in the future [,,].

Excellent ductility is crucial not only for shaping but also for strengthening metals and alloys. The ever most widely used eutectic alloys are suffering from the limited ductility and losing competitiveness among advanced structural materials. Here we report a distinctive concept of phase-selective recrystallization to overcome this challenge for eutectic alloys by triggering the strain hardening capacity of the duplex phases completely. We manipulate the strain partitioning behavior of the two phases in a eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) to obtain the phase-selectively recrystallized microstructure with a fully recrystallized soft phase embedded in the skeleton of a hard phase. The resulting microstructure fully releases the strain hardening capacity in EHEA by eliminating the weak boundaries. Our phase-selectively recrystallized EHEA achieves a high ductility of ∼35% uniform elongation with true stress of ∼2 GPa. This concept is universal for various duplex alloys with soft and hard phases and opens new frontiers for traditional eutectic alloys as high-strength metallic materials. In conclusion, we proposed a universal routine of PSR to ductilize eutectic alloys. The PSR, i.e., individual recrystallization of the soft phase and recovery of the hard phase, was achieved by tailoring the strain partitioning behavior between the two phases of eutectics. Compared with traditional processing methods for eutectic alloys, the PSR prevents premature fracture by eliminating the weak boundaries and thus triggers the intrinsically superior strain hardening capacity of the two phases through dislocation multiplication and potential phase transformation. In a typical FCC/B2 EHEA, ∼35% uniform elongation and ∼2 GPa true stress were achieved. The strain partitioning-dominated PSR mechanism ensures its good adaptability in other duplex alloys, as proven in the A357 alloy. This strategy will open new frontiers of eutectic alloys as high-strength metallic materials in model civilization by combining their excellent castability and strengthening capacity.

drafts.hypothesis: Introducing a minor concentration of a dopant element (e.g., boron) that segregates to the internal phase boundaries in the eutectic high-entropy alloy will modify the interfacial chemistry, facilitating dislocation transmission across lamellar colony boundaries. This should alleviate dislocation pile-ups, reduce local stress concentrations, and thus overcome brittleness while retaining or potentially increasing strength.
drafts.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies that exhibits limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittle failure driven by dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries.
drafts.intervention: Grain boundary doping by adding a minor amount of a dopant (e.g., boron) designed to segregate preferentially to internal phase boundaries.
drafts.conditions: Room-temperature tensile testing under a standard strain rate, with microstructural characterization by electron microscopy post-deformation.
drafts.structural_mediator: Modified interfacial chemistry at the lamellar colony boundaries—thinner or more compliant boundary regions that promote dislocation transmission and reduce the tendency for pile-ups.
drafts.mechanism: The dopant is expected to segregate to the internal boundaries, reducing the barrier for dislocation motion, and thereby enabling more homogeneous plastic flow through controlled boundary sliding or enhanced dislocation transmission. Concurrently, this modification may also yield minor precipitation strengthening effects, maintaining or boosting overall alloy strength.
drafts.predicted_outcome: An increase in room-temperature tensile ductility (potentially in the range of a 10–30% improvement in elongation) while retaining or slightly enhancing yield and ultimate strength relative to the untreated starting material.
drafts.baseline: The untreated eutectic high-entropy alloy, which displays significant dislocation pile-ups at the dual-phase lamellar boundaries that lead to local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic failure.
drafts.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected to be sensitive to the dopant concentration, its uniformity of segregation, and may not translate directly under high-temperature or dynamic loading conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of samples of the eutectic high-entropy alloy with varying minor concentrations of the dopant (e.g., different boron levels). Conduct room-temperature tensile tests to measure yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation to failure. Use high-resolution electron microscopy to image the grain boundaries and assess the distribution and effectiveness of the dopant in altering dislocation behavior. Compare these results to an untreated control sample.
measurements: Tensile stress–strain curves (yield, ultimate tensile strength, elongation)
Electron microscopy images of internal boundaries and dislocation structures
Dopant concentration profiles at the phase boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in ductility (e.g., less than a 10% improvement in elongation) without a reduction in strength, or if microstructural analysis fails to show a reduction in dislocation pile-up at the boundaries, the hypothesis will be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: A tailored post-solidification annealing process that promotes the segregation of a minor ductilizing element to the internal lamellar interfaces in the eutectic high-entropy alloy will form continuous, ductile interfacial layers. These layers can act as dislocation transmission channels to reduce dislocation pile-up, lower local stress concentrations, and suppress microcrack nucleation, thereby markedly increasing room-temperature tensile ductility while retaining or slightly increasing the alloy’s strength.
drafts.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies that exhibits limited room-temperature tensile ductility and a tendency for dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries.
drafts.intervention: Apply a single, targeted post-solidification annealing treatment under controlled atmosphere conditions that is optimized in temperature and time to drive the segregation of a ductile alloying element (already present in the multi-component system or added in small amounts) to the lamellar colony boundaries.
drafts.conditions: Room-temperature tensile loading (strain rate ~0.001/sec) during mechanical testing and standard operating environments; the annealing process is carried out under an inert atmosphere (or vacuum) at a temperature high enough to allow diffusion but below the melting point, followed by controlled cooling.
drafts.structural_mediator: Continuous, segregated ductile interfacial layers at the lamellar boundaries.
drafts.mechanism: The segregated ductile boundary layers will alleviate dislocation pile-ups by serving as transmission channels for dislocations across phases. This mechanism reduces stress concentration at the internal interfaces, thus delaying or preventing microcrack nucleation and propagation under tensile loading.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated starting material, the treated alloy is predicted to exhibit substantially improved ductility (potentially a near doubling of elongation to failure) while maintaining or even slightly increasing its tensile strength, due to the suppression of catastrophic microcrack formation.
drafts.baseline: Untreated eutectic high-entropy alloy that suffers from brittle failure due to dislocation pile-ups near sharp lamellar interfaces.
drafts.boundary: The improvement is contingent on achieving a continuous and effective ductile layer at the interfaces. The processing window (annealing temperature and duration) must be critically controlled; outside these parameters or under extreme strain rates not evaluated here, the beneficial effects may diminish.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens from the same eutectic high-entropy alloy: one set undergoes the proposed post-solidification annealing treatment while the other set serves as a control. Use detailed microstructural analysis (e.g., TEM with STEM-EDS) to verify the formation of continuous ductile layers at the lamellar colony boundaries in the treated specimens. Conduct standardized room-temperature tensile tests (strain rate ~0.001/sec) on both sets and examine dislocation activity in situ or post-mortem via fractography.
measurements: Microstructural characterization of interfacial layers (continuity and thickness via TEM/STEM-EDS)
Fractographic analysis of crack initiation zones and dislocation pile-up patterns
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated specimens do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in tensile ductility (for example, less than a 25% improvement in elongation to failure compared to the control) or if the microstructural analyses do not confirm the formation of continuous ductile interfacial layers, and dislocation pile-ups persist leading to similar or increased localized microcracking, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: A tailored phase‐selective recrystallization treatment that fully recrystallizes the ductile (soft) phase while retaining the hard phase network in the eutectic HEA will reduce dislocation pile‐ups at the lamellar internal boundaries, thereby mitigating local stress concentrations and microcrack initiation, ultimately resulting in improved room-temperature tensile ductility with retained or increased strength.
drafts.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting a hierarchical dual-phase lamellar microstructure (e.g., fcc + B2 colonies) with existing internal phase boundaries that promote dislocation accumulation.
drafts.intervention: Apply a precisely controlled annealing treatment to induce phase-selective recrystallization that targets the ductile phase, refining its grain structure while preserving the integrity of the strengthening hard phase.
drafts.conditions: Quasi-static room-temperature tensile testing with the annealing parameters (temperature and time) optimized to recrystallize only the ductile phase without causing significant coarsening of the hard phase.
drafts.structural_mediator: A refined, recrystallized soft phase with fewer, less detrimental internal boundaries that reduces dislocation pile-ups, embedded in a continuous hard-phase skeleton that contributes to strength.
drafts.mechanism: Selective recrystallization alleviates the stress concentration at the soft/hard phase interfaces by removing excessive dislocation accumulation zones, thus delaying microcrack initiation and enhancing ductility, while the retained hard phase maintains or boosts overall strength.
drafts.predicted_outcome: An increase in uniform elongation (potentially approaching or exceeding 35% compared to lower values in the untreated alloy) and maintenance or even an increase in yield/ultimate tensile strength (approaching true stresses of ~2 GPa) at room temperature.
drafts.baseline: The untreated eutectic HEA exhibits limited tensile ductility and catastrophic failure due to dislocation pile-ups near internal phase boundaries, despite high strength.
drafts.boundary: The success of this intervention is contingent on carefully selected annealing parameters; overly aggressive treatments may lead to undesirable grain growth or loss of the hard phase connectivity, negating the strength benefits.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic HEA samples: one set subjected to the proposed phase-selective annealing treatment and one untreated control group. Characterize the microstructures using TEM and EBSD to verify selective recrystallization of the ductile phase and measure tensile properties using quasi-static room-temperature tensile tests.
measurements: High-resolution imaging (TEM/EBSD) for grain size distribution and phase mapping
Tensile stress-strain curves to determine yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and uniform elongation
Quantitative assessment of dislocation density and pile-up at internal phase boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit a recrystallized soft phase with significantly reduced dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries, or if there is no measurable improvement in ductility and/or if strength is reduced compared to the untreated samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: A brief, controlled annealing treatment designed to trigger phase‐selective recrystallization of the ductile phase within the lamellar microstructure will reduce dislocation pile‐ups at the internal phase boundaries, thereby relieving local stress concentrations and microcracking while retaining or even increasing the overall strength.
drafts.material_initial_state: A eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical dual-phase lamellar structure (e.g., a cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1-type alloy containing alternating ductile FCC and hard B2 lamellae) that exhibits limited room-temperature tensile ductility due to dislocation pile-ups at the interlamellar boundaries.
drafts.intervention: Apply a short-duration, optimized annealing heat treatment (phase-selective recrystallization) that is tailored to preferentially recrystallize the ductile (FCC) phase without coarsening or dissolving the reinforcing hard (B2) phase.
drafts.conditions: Treatment conducted under an inert atmosphere (e.g., argon) with temperature and time settings chosen to promote partial recrystallization at or near the onset of full recrystallization, followed by standard room-temperature tensile testing.
drafts.structural_mediator: A modified microstructure in which the ductile phase has undergone recrystallization to produce refined and more coherent internal boundaries, reducing the sites of dislocation pile-up; the hard phase (B2) remains largely unaltered to maintain or increase strength.
drafts.mechanism: The annealing provides sufficient thermal activation for the ductile phase to recrystallize at its internal boundaries. This relieves the stress concentration caused by dislocation accumulation and minimizes microcrack initiation during straining, while the preserved hard phase continues to contribute to the overall strength.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy is expected to exhibit increased room-temperature tensile ductility (improved elongation to failure) and retention or a slight increase in yield and ultimate tensile strengths relative to the untreated eutectic state.
drafts.baseline: The as-cast eutectic alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies shows limited ductility and a brittle response under tensile loading due to dislocation pile-ups near internal interfaces.
drafts.boundary: The beneficial effects depend on the precise control of annealing temperature and duration; over-annealing may lead to excessive grain growth or coarsening of the lamellae, which could compromise strength, while under-treatment may not sufficiently relieve dislocation pile-ups.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of eutectic HEA samples in the as-cast lamellar state and subject them to a series of annealing treatments varying in temperature and duration. Compare the microstructural evolution (using EBSD/TEM) in the ductile phase and grain boundary characteristics, and then perform room-temperature tensile tests. A control group (no annealing) and an over-annealed group should be included.
measurements: Quantitative analysis of grain size and boundary misorientation in the ductile phase from EBSD/TEM images
Dislocation density mapping in the lamellar colonies
Room-temperature tensile strength and elongation to failure
Fractography to assess microcrack initiation sites
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in tensile ductility (elongation to failure) or if there is a decrease in strength compared to the untreated control, or if microstructural analysis shows no reduction in dislocation pile-ups at the internal boundaries, then the hypothesis that the selective annealing treatment overcomes limited ductility by mitigating internal stress concentrations is falsified.
